GITA NOVEMBER

By: Joy Summers | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
How a Trans gender sex worker became a respected ward secretary of a local town council in a conservative West coast Town

Summary:
They knew she was the right person for the job, but when Gita November’s employers transferred her to take up a key position in HIV-prevention in the West Coast town of Vredenburg, they were somewhat anxious for her safety. Little could they have known that within a couple of months she would completely shift the attitudes of the town’s numerous sex workers towards HIV/Aids. Or that she’d involve herself in all aspects of the community in which she’s now an admired and respected ward council member.

Further information:
Vredenburg is a conservative town near the rapidly expanding port of Saldanha Bay. It is home to workers from the nearby Air Force Base Langebaan, oil installations, and factories like Saldanha Steel. It is also where farm people, local fishermen and sailors go to shop and to look for work. Huge trucks pass through the town. It is a place where hundreds of prostitutes find work.

Gita November, a prostitute who had been working in Beaufort West, was identified, about a year ago, by Sweat (Sex Workers Education and Advocacy Task Force) as the best candidate to set up and run a much-

needed HIV-prevention programme for sex workers in the area. Her personal experience in that tough world, coupled with an inimitable charisma and natural empathy for fellow sex workers, made her an obvious choice to take on the challenge.

“But we were very nervous in the first week; worried she might be physically harmed or assaulted,” said Eugene van Rooyen, Western Cape provincial manager for Sweat, which runs a number of such sites nationwide.

“She had impressed us so much during our interviews and we knew she was the right person for the job. But we were aware that Vredenburg is a very conservative place. The town is dominated by a white, Afrikaans community – and reports were that sex workers were not even permitted on the streets. I was concerned to be sending a transgender, coloured woman, who was a stranger to the community, to go and live and work there.

“But, within a week of her arrival, she let me know she had found accommodation and had already made friends. Within a couple of weeks, she had been accepted by the community, had set up the site and sorted out the police. There was no unpleasantness and no problem.”That was about a year ago. Since then, said Van Rooyen, the Sweat management had been astounded at the progress November has made in the district.

As site coordinator, November was tasked with organising workshops and regular health screenings for sex workers, as well as managing a team of peer educators to help them with their problems. Part of the job is to work closely with the local health services and the police.

“When she started, the local sex workers never went to the clinics or took HIV tests because of the stigma,” said Sweat director Maria Stacey. “They were also regularly victims of crime but too scared to go to police. Now they test willingly every three months and it is their mission to stay negative.

“The madam of the local brothel wanted to kill her when the project started but is now herself a proud peer educator, has painted and cleaned up the brothel and reduced her tik use. One of the sex workers has enrolled in night school and wants to get her matric. Others want to follow suit.”

Not long after November arrived in Vredenburg, Van Rooyen decided to drive up and attend her first risk reduction workshop.

“There was Gita, dressed in a pencil skirt, her hair beautiful, with all the sex workers sitting around, listening to her, riveted. They were talking freely to her… she had created an absolutely amazing environment for them. At the end of that workshop, they made a group decision to be tested. That, for us, was amazing.”

November then arranged for the nursing sister from the state clinic – with whom she had already established a relationship – to do the testing. “Afterwards, the nurse was quite emotional, overwhelmed,” said Van Rooyen. “She told us that for the past five years she had been trying to engage with sex workers to be tested at the clinic. She could not believe that, in one day, they were all getting tested.

“You had sex workers on one side – and the community, the clinics and the police on the other…“Gita started talking to the police and the clinics and other community members… and, essentially, she succeeded in breaking down the divisions. In fact, the police and the clinics were dying to cooperate but the sex workers thought the police were the enemy and that the clinics were the last place to go with a problem.”

Before long, through November’s efforts, sex workers were cooperating with the police and, when they were victims of crime, reporting incidents to the police, which they’d never done before.

“The disrespect is simply not there anymore,” said Van Rooyen.

November soon became involved in other community issues like drug use, unemployment and corruption in the Vredenburg CBD (Ward 8) where most of the sex workers operate.

“She simply became involved in all aspects of the town… and soon she was being invited to functions with the mayor (Francois Scheepers of the DA). She is a networker of note. Whenever a big issue arises, November is there,” said Van Rooyen.

About six months ago November, who is an openly transgender sex worker – who still services clients in between doing her job – was appointed secretary to the ward management committee of Ward 8. She has also been nominated as a councillor.

“We work directly with the community and feed back to the ward councillors. We listen to all their problems. I attend all municipal meetings,” said November.

“It is the perfect ward for me to be part of. There are numerous social issues that need to be dealt with – including crime and unemployment. We need a hospice and we need to bring an end to discrimination when local people try to access health services,” November told Noseweek.

Ward councillors and sex workers alike sang November’s praises when Noseweek visited Vredenburg. November walked into the meeting in heels and a mini and flashed a disarming smile that somehow pulled the room together.

Vanessa Taylor, a ward committee member working on the West Coast HIV/Aids initiative, said: “November’s interactions at different levels in the community are changing mindsets and having a huge impact on the spread and prevention of HIV. There is education and awareness now but also, for the sex workers, there is suddenly a sense of dignity and of belonging. They have found a voice through somebody who does not discriminate against them and who gives them a space in society, accepting them for who they are.

Fellow ward committee members Sandra Marcus and Gina Korah agreed: “Before my encounters with Gita November, I had nothing but disrespect for sex workers, but she gave us such an education. My husband and I now see these young women as family. Now when I see them, I stop and chat. They have become our children,” said Korah.

Press Release:


Gita November
She applies makeup, brushes back her shoulder-length hair and slips effortlessly into stiletto heels before another day's work. Gita November is a site co-ordinator for SWEAT and she's changing the lives of sex workers on the margins of society. But that's her day job. Gita is also a transgender sex worker. In a candid interview about her struggles to overcome prejudice, amusing anecdotes about her sex work, and how she has found meaning in her new role protecting sex workers from police brutality and the ravages of HIV, Gita shows Carte Blanche how anyone can triumph, no matter the hurdles they must overcome


Script:


GITA NOVEMBER FINAL SCRIPT

Gita
I see myself as a heterosexual female trapped in a mans body

Commentary One
Christened Marchand November, Gita November tried for 18 years to conform to the family she really loved, but in the end she chose life on her own terms

Gita
So I would rather live, as to exist. Its either I am living- but I am not going to exist in your frame of how you want me to be

Commentary Two
Gita is trans gender. Seven years ago she went through her final transformation-out went the short hair and suits and in came the hats and heels

Gita
So I went to church with a hat on – so I posted a picture on Facebook
Knowing full well that my family is friends with me on Facebook.

Devi
Oh Gita you know how to court trouble

Gita
I was disowned from the family. My family just went bonkers, how could I bring such shame over the family?

Commentary Three
Born in the Karoo town of Sutherland- her family was strict members of the old apostolic church there

Devi
Growing up in a small town what did that feel like?
Gita
Suffocating
Devi
Did people make you feel like there was something wrong with you?


Gita
Yes all the time. They made me feel like as if I was a virus. Everyone was looking for a cure, to cure you

Devi Link
Gita’s childhood was difficult and confusing but when she eventually established her identity she finally felt she belonged

GITA
I don’t give people power over me. I refuse that
Devi
How do you get used to people deciding what you are
Gita
I just ignore it. Back in the day I would go all gangster on them, it’s like what are you looking at- and then no this is not ladylike and I just decided this is not a part of me

Commentary four
But what most people don’t know is that Gita is also a sex worker- a secret she kept from her family

GITA
I sell a service and the reason why they come to me is because the service is good.

Commentary Five
That secret life began in Cape Town as a homesick adolescent- where she met a man at a river who paid her for sexual favours.

But you didn’t see this as sex work
Devi
NO! I saw him as my river boyfriend

Commentary Six
After school Gita got a job in the call centre of a long distance bus service
Gita
I would flirt with the guys over the phone
Devi
They wanted bus tickets and what would you give them in return?
Gita
And then I decided but I don’t want to work in the call centre I want to work on the bus

Commentary Seven
So Gita became a steward on the OVERNIGHT BUS

GITA
That was also difficult because in the call centre I could be GITA, but in the road I had to be Marchand and I had to cut my hair-but you know what I did, I would put on my female pants but a male shirt hang over.

Devi
But Gita wouldn’t the passengers get confused you start as one thing at the front of the journey…

Gita
Ya know I would wear make up and everything

Commentary Eight
Gita used her charm on the bus service with profitable results.

Gita
So when the people get on the bus I would scan them
Devi
But how do you scan who is going to be interested or not?
Gita
When you seat them you touch them in a way and they will touch you back and then…
Devi
its on
Gita
Okay it’s on

Commentary nine
Gita carefully planned that after she put the lights out she was seated next to her prospective client.

Gita
Then I would relocate them, and I will switch off the lights – and then put the blanket on me – and then later on I would switch on the air con so he would get cold and then I would share my blanket with him and from there on …it will start


Devi
So let me get this straight there are guys that want guys that are pretty like you
Yes
Many?
Gita
A lot!
Devi
Because your energy is very female …cos we’re chatting like too girls here
Yes
Did you ever have instances where the guys realize what the actual situation was?
A lot!

Commentary eleven
In Beaufort West she plied her trade to the passing truck drivers, But here she also began to educate other sex workers about HIV. It would be a step that would soon change Gita’s life

LINK
We are here for you 24 /7, that’s Sweats promise to sex workers and its here that Gita’s potential was recognized

EUGENE
She understands all the complexities of the people she is trying to help
And because of that understanding, people trust her

Commentary Twelve
Eugene Van Rooyen is Sweats Western Cape provincial manager.

Eugene
One of our biggest objectives is to get sex work decriminalized in SA

Commentary thirteen
But SWEAT also assist sex workers on the periphery and is firmly in their corner. They sent Gita to a national sex workers symposium in Sandton where she told her story

Gita
And that was the first time that I came out saying publicly that I am a sex workers…Ok it cost a lot of family members but if I could go back and do it again I would do it.

Commentary Fourteen
About 60 % of South Africa’s sex workers are HIV positive –it’s a figure that SWEAT is determined to reduce. As part of their effort, Eugene needed leaders in the small towns. When he interviewed Gita he wanted to send her to Vredenburg

EUGENE
I immediately knew this was the right person for the job, however I was very worried because even the staff were harassed by the police

Commentary Fifteen
Vredenburg is a conservative West coast town – Eugene was concerned it’s hardly the place to send a trans gender sex worker to change hardened attitudes

Devi
When you were told that you were coming to Vredenburg were you scared?
Gita
Yes I was.
Gita
I took the taxi and I thought… where am I going?

Commentary sixteen
Her reception on Vredenburg’s streets wasn’t exactly welcoming as sex worker Salome Hernis explains

Salome
The girl with the beautiful body and we wanted to attack her
Devi
Did you think she was mad in the beginning?
Salome
We were thinking oh what a girl is this – we were only thinking about our clients
Devi
So in your mind she was Competition
Salome
and she said I am not coming to take your spot, and then she tell us about sweat

EUGENE
And I think within a week she had organized the whole town

LINK
For Gita it’s all about restoring the dignity of sex workers

Commentary Seventeen
Dignity, she says that was not respected by the police when she arrived

GITA
They would stand there and they would literally chase them away like animals.

Commentary eighteen
Within months of arriving Gita had been voted as chairperson of a forum called breaking the silence – at one of its meetings she brought the police on board

GITA
I got a DVD and I played them the stories about sex workers and police brutality and that day they vowed – we will look after the sex workers in the West coast

LINK
So one of her tasks was to get sex workers tested …before Gita arrived that wasn’t happening

Commentary nineteen
The sex workers refused to go to the clinics because of gossiping nurses

GITA
They would go around and say to everyone in the community you know that one is HIV positive
Devi
The whole story!
Gita
No wonder…

Commentary twenty
They felt the nurses were prejudiced

Gita
And they would say why do you come and test for HIV – you already have it, because already you are sleeping with all the men in road.

Commentary twenty- one
Undeterred, Gita convinced them to get tested at workshops she held at their private homes.

Gita
I would lead the space, get them to participate how they feel about it.

Commentary twenty-two
Health workers had failed for five years to convince the sex workers to get tested. Comparatively Gita’s stats in 12 months are remarkable

DEVI
How many
GITA
More than about 180
Devi
That was from 0
Gita from 0 to 180

Salome
Now there is a BIG difference- Gita sends TB testing to our place, we had never done that before

Up sound singing at workshop
My mother was a kitchen girl, my father was a garden boy that is why I am a sex worker, a sex worker, a sex worker…

Commentary Twenty- one
Once a month Gita organizes a creative space workshop. It’s a place where someone finally listens - where sex workers find respect.

Eugene
The beauty of it is that we can learn from this because if I had those reservations and she didn’t get the job we wouldn’t have had this wonderful success

Commentary Twenty-two
These days Gita is really busy – she has been voted in as a ward secretary for the CBD. She has future political ambitions, she is managing a team of peer educators and she still has to find time for her clients

Devi
Do you think you will ever retire?
Gita
It would be difficult I love my job but I will still have the one sideline client
Devi
Just the one
Gita
Just the one! Who is going to give them the good service, I am concerned about that?

Devi
I am sure a lot of people want to ask you this and I am going to ask you- do you want to become a woman?
Gita
I am satisfied – I don’t want to go for the operation- cutting off a genital part doesn’t define who I am. I am Gita and that is me!
Devi
She is here to stay
Gita
SHE IS!

THE END

Back in the day I would go all gangster on them, it’s like what are you looking at- and then no this is not ladylike and I just decided this is not a part of me Commentary four But what most people don’t know is that Gita is also a sex worker- a secret she kept from her family GITA I sell a service and the reason why they come to me is because the service is good. Commentary Five That secret life began in Cape Town as a homesick adolescent- where she met a man at a river who paid her for sexual favours. But you didn’t see this as sex work Devi NO! I saw him as my river boyfriend Commentary Six After school Gita got a job in the call centre of a long distance bus service Gita I would flirt with the guys over the phone Devi They wanted bus tickets and what would you give them in return? Gita And then I decided but I don’t want to work in the call centre I want to work on the bus Commentary Seven So Gita became a steward on the OVERNIGHT BUS GITA That was also difficult because in the call centre I could be GITA, but in the road I had to be Marchand and I had to cut my hair-but you know what I did, I would put on my female pants but a male shirt hang over. Devi But Gita wouldn’t the passengers get confused you start as one thing at the front of the journey… Gita Ya know I would wear make up and everything Commentary Eight Gita used her charm on the bus service with profitable results. Gita So when the people get on the bus I would scan them Devi But how do you scan who is going to be interested or not? Gita When you seat them you touch them in a way and they will touch you back and then… Devi its on Gita Okay it’s on Commentary nine Gita carefully planned that after she put the lights out she was seated next to her prospective client. Gita Then I would relocate them, and I will switch off the lights – and then put the blanket on me – and then later on I would switch on the air con so he would get cold and then I would share my blanket with him and from there on …it will start Devi So let me get this straight there are guys that want guys that are pretty like you Yes Many? Gita A lot! Devi Because your energy is very female …cos we’re chatting like too girls here Yes Did you ever have instances where the guys realize what the actual situation was? A lot! Commentary eleven In Beaufort West she plied her trade to the passing truck drivers, But here she also began to educate other sex workers about HIV. It would be a step that would soon change Gita’s life LINK We are here for you 24 /7, that’s Sweats promise to sex workers and its here that Gita’s potential was recognized EUGENE She understands all the complexities of the people she is trying to help And because of that understanding, people trust her Commentary Twelve Eugene Van Rooyen is Sweats Western Cape provincial manager. Eugene One of our biggest objectives is to get sex work decriminalized in SA Commentary thirteen But SWEAT also assist sex workers on the periphery and is firmly in their corner. They sent Gita to a national sex workers symposium in Sandton where she told her story Gita And that was the first time that I came out saying publicly that I am a sex workers…Ok it cost a lot of family members but if I could go back and do it again I would do it. Commentary Fourteen About 60 % of South Africa’s sex workers are HIV positive –it’s a figure that SWEAT is determined to reduce. As part of their effort, Eugene needed leaders in the small towns. When he interviewed Gita he wanted to send her to Vredenburg EUGENE I immediately knew this was the right person for the job, however I was very worried because even the staff were harassed by the police Commentary Fifteen Vredenburg is a conservative West coast town – Eugene was concerned it’s hardly the place to send a trans gender sex worker to change hardened attitudes Devi When you were told that you were coming to Vredenburg were you scared? Gita Yes I was. Gita I took the taxi and I thought… where am I going? Commentary sixteen Her reception on Vredenburg’s streets wasn’t exactly welcoming as sex worker Salome Hernis explains Salome The girl with the beautiful body and we wanted to attack her Devi Did you think she was mad in the beginning? Salome We were thinking oh what a girl is this – we were only thinking about our clients Devi So in your mind she was Competition Salome and she said I am not coming to take your spot, and then she tell us about sweat EUGENE And I think within a week she had organized the whole town LINK For Gita it’s all about restoring the dignity of sex workers Commentary Seventeen Dignity, she says that was not respected by the police when she arrived GITA They would stand there and they would literally chase them away like animals. Commentary eighteen Within months of arriving Gita had been voted as chairperson of a forum called breaking the silence – at one of its meetings she brought the police on board GITA I got a DVD and I played them the stories about sex workers and police brutality and that day they vowed – we will look after the sex workers in the West coast LINK So one of her tasks was to get sex workers tested …before Gita arrived that wasn’t happening Commentary nineteen The sex workers refused to go to the clinics because of gossiping nurses GITA They would go around and say to everyone in the community you know that one is HIV positive Devi The whole story! Gita No wonder… Commentary twenty They felt the nurses were prejudiced Gita And they would say why do you come and test for HIV – you already have it, because already you are sleeping with all the men in road. Commentary twenty- one Undeterred, Gita convinced them to get tested at workshops she held at their private homes. Gita I would lead the space, get them to participate how they feel about it. Commentary twenty-two Health workers had failed for five years to convince the sex workers to get tested. Comparatively Gita’s stats in 12 months are remarkable DEVI How many GITA More than about 180 Devi That was from 0 Gita from 0 to 180 Salome Now there is a BIG difference- Gita sends TB testing to our place, we had never done that before Up sound singing at workshop My mother was a kitchen girl, my father was a garden boy that is why I am a sex worker, a sex worker, a sex worker… Commentary Twenty- one Once a month Gita organizes a creative space workshop. It’s a place where someone finally listens - where sex workers find respect. Eugene The beauty of it is that we can learn from this because if I had those reservations and she didn’t get the job we wouldn’t have had this wonderful success Commentary Twenty-two These days Gita is really busy – she has been voted in as a ward secretary for the CBD. She has future political ambitions, she is managing a team of peer educators and she still has to find time for her clients Devi Do you think you will ever retire? Gita It would be difficult I love my job but I will still have the one sideline client Devi Just the one Gita Just the one! Who is going to give them the good service, I am concerned about that? Devi I am sure a lot of people want to ask you this and I am going to ask you- do you want to become a woman? Gita I am satisfied – I don’t want to go for the operation- cutting off a genital part doesn’t define who I am. I am Gita and that is me! Devi She is here to stay Gita SHE IS! metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): How a Trans gender sex worker became a respected ward secretary of a local town council in a conservative West coast Town
metadata.Summary: They knew she was the right person for the job, but when Gita November’s employers transferred her to take up a key position in HIV-prevention in the West Coast town of Vredenburg, they were somewhat anxious for her safety. Little could they have known that within a couple of months she would completely shift the attitudes of the town’s numerous sex workers towards HIV/Aids. Or that she’d involve herself in all aspects of the community in which she’s now an admired and respected ward council member.
metadata.Further information: Vredenburg is a conservative town near the rapidly expanding port of Saldanha Bay. It is home to workers from the nearby Air Force Base Langebaan, oil installations, and factories like Saldanha Steel. It is also where farm people, local fishermen and sailors go to shop and to look for work. Huge trucks pass through the town. It is a place where hundreds of prostitutes find work. Gita November, a prostitute who had been working in Beaufort West, was identified, about a year ago, by Sweat (Sex Workers Education and Advocacy Task Force) as the best candidate to set up and run a much- needed HIV-prevention programme for sex workers in the area. Her personal experience in that tough world, coupled with an inimitable charisma and natural empathy for fellow sex workers, made her an obvious choice to take on the challenge. “But we were very nervous in the first week; worried she might be physically harmed or assaulted,” said Eugene van Rooyen, Western Cape provincial manager for Sweat, which runs a number of such sites nationwide. “She had impressed us so much during our interviews and we knew she was the right person for the job. But we were aware that Vredenburg is a very conservative place. The town is dominated by a white, Afrikaans community – and reports were that sex workers were not even permitted on the streets. I was concerned to be sending a transgender, coloured woman, who was a stranger to the community, to go and live and work there. “But, within a week of her arrival, she let me know she had found accommodation and had already made friends. Within a couple of weeks, she had been accepted by the community, had set up the site and sorted out the police. There was no unpleasantness and no problem.”That was about a year ago. Since then, said Van Rooyen, the Sweat management had been astounded at the progress November has made in the district. As site coordinator, November was tasked with organising workshops and regular health screenings for sex workers, as well as managing a team of peer educators to help them with their problems. Part of the job is to work closely with the local health services and the police. “When she started, the local sex workers never went to the clinics or took HIV tests because of the stigma,” said Sweat director Maria Stacey. “They were also regularly victims of crime but too scared to go to police. Now they test willingly every three months and it is their mission to stay negative. “The madam of the local brothel wanted to kill her when the project started but is now herself a proud peer educator, has painted and cleaned up the brothel and reduced her tik use. One of the sex workers has enrolled in night school and wants to get her matric. Others want to follow suit.” Not long after November arrived in Vredenburg, Van Rooyen decided to drive up and attend her first risk reduction workshop. “There was Gita, dressed in a pencil skirt, her hair beautiful, with all the sex workers sitting around, listening to her, riveted. They were talking freely to her… she had created an absolutely amazing environment for them. At the end of that workshop, they made a group decision to be tested. That, for us, was amazing.” November then arranged for the nursing sister from the state clinic – with whom she had already established a relationship – to do the testing. “Afterwards, the nurse was quite emotional, overwhelmed,” said Van Rooyen. “She told us that for the past five years she had been trying to engage with sex workers to be tested at the clinic. She could not believe that, in one day, they were all getting tested. “You had sex workers on one side – and the community, the clinics and the police on the other…“Gita started talking to the police and the clinics and other community members… and, essentially, she succeeded in breaking down the divisions. In fact, the police and the clinics were dying to cooperate but the sex workers thought the police were the enemy and that the clinics were the last place to go with a problem.” Before long, through November’s efforts, sex workers were cooperating with the police and, when they were victims of crime, reporting incidents to the police, which they’d never done before. “The disrespect is simply not there anymore,” said Van Rooyen. November soon became involved in other community issues like drug use, unemployment and corruption in the Vredenburg CBD (Ward 8) where most of the sex workers operate. “She simply became involved in all aspects of the town… and soon she was being invited to functions with the mayor (Francois Scheepers of the DA). She is a networker of note. Whenever a big issue arises, November is there,” said Van Rooyen. About six months ago November, who is an openly transgender sex worker – who still services clients in between doing her job – was appointed secretary to the ward management committee of Ward 8. She has also been nominated as a councillor. “We work directly with the community and feed back to the ward councillors. We listen to all their problems. I attend all municipal meetings,” said November. “It is the perfect ward for me to be part of. There are numerous social issues that need to be dealt with – including crime and unemployment. We need a hospice and we need to bring an end to discrimination when local people try to access health services,” November told Noseweek. Ward councillors and sex workers alike sang November’s praises when Noseweek visited Vredenburg. November walked into the meeting in heels and a mini and flashed a disarming smile that somehow pulled the room together. Vanessa Taylor, a ward committee member working on the West Coast HIV/Aids initiative, said: “November’s interactions at different levels in the community are changing mindsets and having a huge impact on the spread and prevention of HIV. There is education and awareness now but also, for the sex workers, there is suddenly a sense of dignity and of belonging. They have found a voice through somebody who does not discriminate against them and who gives them a space in society, accepting them for who they are. Fellow ward committee members Sandra Marcus and Gina Korah agreed: “Before my encounters with Gita November, I had nothing but disrespect for sex workers, but she gave us such an education. My husband and I now see these young women as family. Now when I see them, I stop and chat. They have become our children,” said Korah.
